newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan Taleban demands seat at Islamic summit.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban demands seat at Islamic summit.

text.p: The Islamic Taleban movement on Saturday demanded Afghanistan's empty seat at a summit meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Conference (OIC).

"We control more than 80 percent of the country's area where we have restored peace," Mufti Masoom Afghani, ambassador at the Taleban-controlled Afghan embassy in Islamabad, told a news conference. "Therefore, we deserve to be given the seat of Afghanistan in the OIC in accordance with international norms."
A Taleban delegation led by Mullah Mohammad Rabbani, chairman of the militia's ruling interim council, arrived in Islamabad on Friday to try to attend Sunday's summit.

Pakistan says the Taleban will not be able to take up Afghanistan's seat because the OIC adopted a "vacant-seat policy" after the overthrow of the former government led by President Burhanuddin Rabbani in September.
"The seat in the OIC is our right. This seat should be given to us. Keeping Afghanistan out of OIC is unjust," Afghani said.

He said the Taleban was surprised that claims by Rabbani's government to be recognised as legitimate were still entertained by the OIC, the United States and international organisations even though it did not control the capital, Kabul.
"It is surprising that those who have restored peace in the war-torn country are not being recognised," he said. "The OIC has no satisfactory reason."
Afghani asked OIC members to open their embassies in Kabul and let the Taleban take over embassies in their countries.
He said the Taleban had pacified the country, stopped drug smuggling and collected weapons. "We have taken back arms from unauthorised people and restored the rule of Islamic law.

"From Salang Pass to Herat, anyone can move freely without any fear and without being looted or checked," he said. "On the other hand, areas controlled by our opponents are not safe and people are looted and subjected to torture."

He accused Russia, India, Uzbekistan and Iran of backing anti-Taleban forces. "There are indications that Uzbekistan supports (northern opposition leader) General Abdul Rasheed Dostum. Iran, Russia and India also support our opponents."
Afghani said the opposition groups were divided and areas they controlled would soon fall to the Taleban.

"Things have reached a stage where Dostum is himself leading his troops on the front, no one knows where Rabbani lives, while (former government commander) Ahmad Shah Masood is trying to escape to Tajikistan," he said.

Afghani said the Taleban did not want to meddle in other countries and demanded that this policy be reciprocated. "We neither interfere in the affairs of any other country nor will we allow anyone else to interfere in our affairs," he said.
Afghani denied reports that the Taleban was holding 31 men from Pakistan's Anti-Narcotics Force (ANF) who had chased drug smugglers across the border into Afghanistan.
"They might have been taken to somewhere else but not into Afghanistan," he said. "Gone are the days when kidnapped people were taken to Afghanistan. Now no one can dare to do it."

Officials in the Pakistani border city of Quetta said on Saturday that Afghan consulate officials and the head of the ANF had gone to the Afghan town of Lashkargarh, about 10 km (six miles) inside the border, to try to obtain the release of the Pakistanis, who they said had been detained on Friday.
